title: Joshua's Commission and the Song of Moses

date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Moses was 120 years old, could no more go out and come in, and would not go over Jordan, because the LORD had said so (Deut 31:2).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:2, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The LORD would go over before Israel and destroy the nations as he did Sihon and Og, kings of the Amorites, and Joshua would go over before them as the LORD had said (Deut 31:3–4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:3–4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Moses charged the people, "Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee" (Deut 31:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Moses called Joshua and charged him in the sight of all Israel to go with the people into the land sworn to their fathers and cause them to inherit it, with the LORD going before him and not failing or forsaking him (Deut 31:7–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:7–8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Joshua had already been publicly designated as Moses' successor: the LORD told Moses to lay his hand on Joshua, a man in whom is the spirit, set him before Eleazar and the congregation, and give him a charge in their sight (Num 27:18–23); Deut 3:28 records the command to charge, encourage, and strengthen Joshua.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 3:28, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); KJV Num 27:18–23, read in full via the Preview API.

claims.claim: Moses wrote "this law" and delivered it to the priests, the sons of Levi who bore the ark of the covenant, and to all the elders of Israel (Deut 31:9).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 31:9 (read in full: the two-copy contract practice, Jer 32:12–14, as analogy).

claims.claim: The scope of "this law" in Deut 31:9 — the whole book of Deuteronomy, or the part contained in chapters 27–30 — is not settled by the text.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 31:9 (read in full: "either the whole book of Deuteronomy, or the important part of it contained between the twenty-seventh and thirtieth chapters"); K&D on Deut 31 (read in full: the writing out of the laws, without narrowing the scope in the passage read).

claims.claim: At the end of every seven years, in the year of release, at the Feast of Tabernacles, the law was to be read before all Israel — men, women, children, and the stranger within the gates — so that they might hear, learn, fear the LORD, and observe all the words of the law, and their children might hear and learn (Deut 31:10–13).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:10–13, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The LORD summoned Moses and Joshua to present themselves in the tabernacle of the congregation that he might give Joshua a charge, and appeared in a pillar of cloud standing over the door of the tabernacle (Deut 31:14–15).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:14–15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 31:14–15 (read in full: confirmation of the Num 27 designation; manifestation at the door, since only priests entered the sanctuary).

claims.claim: The LORD foretold that after Moses slept with his fathers, Israel would rise up, go whoring after the gods of the strangers of the land, forsake him, and break his covenant, and that he would hide his face from them (Deut 31:16–18, 20, 29).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:16–18, 20, 29, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). (The text's prediction; its fulfilment in any specific later event is not claimed here.)

claims.claim: The Song was commissioned as a witness against Israel: Moses was to write it, teach it to the children of Israel, and put it in their mouths, so that it would testify against them when evils befell them, for it would not be forgotten out of the mouths of their seed (Deut 31:19, 21–22).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:19, 21–22, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 31:19 (read in full: national songs take deep hold of the memory).

claims.claim: The LORD himself gave Joshua a charge distinct from Moses' charge: "thou shalt bring the children of Israel into the land which I sware unto them: and I will be with thee" (Deut 31:23).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:23, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: When Moses had finished writing the words of the law in a book, he commanded the Levites who bore the ark to take the book of the law and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant, to be there for a witness against Israel, because of their rebellion and stiff neck (Deut 31:24–27).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:24–27, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on Deut 31:24–27 (read in full: "put it by the side of the ark"; "the Levites" as the Levitical priests).

claims.claim: Whether the book was deposited beside the ark (in a chest by it) or within the ark is not settled: 1 Kgs 8:9 says the ark contained only the tables of stone, while Heb 9:4 attests other things once inside it.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 31:26 (read in full: both readings recorded); K&D on Deut 31:24–27 (read in full: "by the side of the ark").

claims.claim: Moses gathered all the elders of the tribes and their officers, spoke the words in their ears, and called heaven and earth to record against them (Deut 31:28).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:28, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Moses spoke the words of the Song in the ears of all the congregation of Israel until they were ended (Deut 31:30), and again with Hoshea the son of Nun (Deut 32:44).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 31:30; 32:44, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The Song opens by summoning heaven to give ear and earth to hear, compares doctrine to rain and dew on grass, and calls on the hearers to ascribe greatness to God (Deut 32:1–3).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:1–3, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 32:1 (read in full: the exordium's magnificence).

claims.claim: God is the Rock, his work perfect, all his ways judgment, a God of truth without iniquity, just and right (Deut 32:4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 32:4 (read in full: Rock as power and stability, true to covenant).

claims.claim: Israel corrupted themselves; "their spot is not the spot of his children: they are a perverse and crooked generation" (Deut 32:5), and Moses asks, "Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise?" (Deut 32:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:5–6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The Song commands remembrance: "Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations: ask thy father, and he will shew thee; thy elders, and they will tell thee" (Deut 32:7).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:7, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The Masoretic Text of Deut 32:8 reads "sons of Israel" (בני ישראל; KJV "children of Israel").
claims.evidence: Anselm Project (read in full: MT/Westminster Leningrad Codex בני ישראל); KJV Deut 32:8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The Qumran scroll 4QDeut-j (c. 1st century BCE) reads "sons of God" (בני אלהים) at Deut 32:8, and the Septuagint reflects divine/angelic beings: most Greek manuscripts "angels of God," a few "sons of God" (the Göttingen text adopts "sons of God").
claims.evidence: Anselm Project, read in full (all three witness readings stated explicitly); NETS Deut 32:8, read in full ("according to the number of divine sons"). Heiser 2001, read in full (re-grounding session 2026-11-20; gilberthouse.org PDF of Bibliotheca Sacra 158, 52–74): two Qumran manuscripts; Wevers, Göttingen, p. 347 — the excerpts previously cited are verified accurate.

claims.claim: A reconstructed original "sons of El" (בני אל) at Deut 32:8 is a scholarly conjecture, NOT a manuscript reading: no witness reads בני אל.
claims.evidence: Shared record §2.3 (methodological statement on the witnesses in clm-deu-09-021–022); Anselm Project, read in full (no witness listed reads בני אל).

claims.claim: Explanations of the 32:8 variant by editorial motive — e.g. copyists softening a polytheistic wording, or the LXX "angels" reading as a deliberate avoidance of lesser deities — are hypotheses about scribal intention, not attested events.
claims.evidence: Nilsen, read in full ("copyists changed the words to make the verse less polytheistic" offered as explanation); Heiser 2001, read in full (re-grounding session 2026-11-20): Wevers: the majority LXX reading "clearly a later attempt to avoid any notion of lesser deities". No ancient source attests the motive.

claims.claim: The priority of the readings at 32:8 is disputed: most scholars (as Nilsen reports) regard "children of God/gods" as probably the best reading, while Keil & Delitzsch (pre-Qumran) judged the LXX "angels of God" rendering "of no critical value."
claims.evidence: Nilsen, read in full; K&D on Deut 32:8, read in full (the LXX rendering "nothing more than an arbitrary interpretation," founded on the guardian-angels notion, Sir. 17:14).

claims.claim: "For the LORD's portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance" (Deut 32:9).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The LORD found Jacob in a desert land and waste howling wilderness, led him about, instructed him, kept him as the apple of his eye, and bore him as an eagle bears its young on its wings; the LORD alone led him, with no strange god (Deut 32:10–12).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:10–12, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 32:11 (read in full: the eagle's care); Clarke on Deut 32:11 (read in full: ירחף, "broodeth over").

claims.claim: The LORD made Israel ride on the high places, eat the increase of the fields, suck honey from the rock and oil from the flinty rock, with butter, milk, fat of lambs and rams of Bashan, and the pure blood of the grape (Deut 32:13–14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:13–14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 32:13–14 (read in full: the trans-Jordanic setting of the imagery).

claims.claim: "But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked… then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation" (Deut 32:15); Jeshurun is the poetic name for Israel, from yashar ("upright") — "the upright."
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (the text-fact); Clarke on Deut 32:15 (read in full: Jeshurun = "the upright," from ישר) for the gloss — a commentary reading, hence Probable overall.

claims.claim: Israel provoked God to jealousy with strange gods and abominations, and "sacrificed unto devils, not to God; to gods whom they knew not, to new gods that came newly up, whom your fathers feared not," forgetting the Rock that begat them (Deut 32:16–18).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:16–18, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The LORD abhorred them, said he would hide his face from them, and would move them to jealousy with those who are not a people and provoke them with a foolish nation, as they had moved him to jealousy with what is not God (Deut 32:19–21).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:19–21, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: A fire kindled in God's anger burns to the lowest hell; he will heap mischiefs, spend arrows, send hunger, burning heat, bitter destruction, teeth of beasts, poison of serpents, sword without and terror within (Deut 32:22–25).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:22–25, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The LORD said he would scatter Israel into corners and make their remembrance cease, were it not that he feared the wrath of the enemy, lest their adversaries say, "Our hand is high, and the LORD hath not done all this" (Deut 32:26–27).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:26–27, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "O that they were wise, that they understood this, that they would consider their latter end! How should one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, except their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had shut them up?" (Deut 32:28–30).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:28–30, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "For their rock is not as our Rock, even our enemies themselves being judges. For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the fields of Gomorrah: their grapes are grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter: their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps" (Deut 32:31–33).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:31–33, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste" (Deut 32:35).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:35, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "For the LORD shall judge his people, and repent himself for his servants, when he seeth that their power is gone, and there is none shut up, or left" (Deut 32:36).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:36, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The LORD challenges the false gods: "Where are their gods, their rock in whom they trusted, which did eat the fat of their sacrifices, and drank the wine of their drink offerings? let them rise up and help you, and be your protection" (Deut 32:37–38).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:37–38, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal: neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand. For I lift up my hand to heaven, and say, I live for ever" (Deut 32:39–40).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:39–40, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The LORD will whet his glittering sword, take hold on judgment, render vengeance to his enemies, make his arrows drunk with blood, and his sword devour flesh (Deut 32:41–42).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:41–42, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The Masoretic Text HAS Deut 32:43, in a shorter form: "Rejoice, O ye nations, with his people: for he will avenge the blood of his servants, and will render vengeance to his adversaries, and will be merciful unto his land, and to his people." It does not omit the verse.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:43, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (the verse is present, four cola).

claims.claim: The verse is commonly counted at four cola in the MT, six in 4QDeut-q, and eight in the LXX.
claims.evidence: NETS Deut 32:43, read in full (eight cola counted directly); the MT four and the 4QDeut-q six as stated in the Academia DSS overview (Feldman, read in full, re-grounding session 2026-11-20): "the equally often cited six-colae wording of Deut 32:43 in 4QDeutq (cf. the four cola of the MT and the eight of the LXX; Rofé 2002: 47-54)"; 4QDeut-q (4Q44; 50–1 BCE). DJD XIV still not read (see shared record §1), and Nilsen describes both the MT and Qumran forms as "quite short." Hence Probable, not Established.

claims.claim: The longer forms of 32:43 are not identical to each other: 4QDeut-q opens with the heavens rejoicing and "all gods" (אלהים) bowing down, while the LXX has "all the divine sons" doing obeisance and "all the angels of God" prevailing, combining material from both shorter forms.
claims.evidence: Nilsen, read in full (Qumran "all gods" vs LXX "children of God"; "The Septuagint combines both"); NETS Deut 32:43, read in full. Probable because the 4QDeut-q wording itself was not directly inspected (DJD XIV not read).

claims.claim: Hebrews 1:6 ("And let all the angels of God worship him") follows the longer Greek/Qumran text-form of Deut 32:43, not the MT, whose verse contains no angels and no worship summons to heavenly beings.
claims.evidence: KJV Heb 1:6, read in full via BibleGateway KJV pages; NETS Deut 32:43, read in full (divine sons obeisance; angels prevail); Nilsen, read in full. Probable because the exact wording is an adaptation (clm-deu-09-045).

claims.claim: The exact Hebrews 1:6 wording ("angels of God" + "worship") is not verbatim in NETS Deut 32:43 as a single colon, and Psalm 97:7 ("worship him, all ye gods") is a live alternative source for the quotation; which passage Hebrews draws on is not settled.
claims.evidence: NETS Deut 32:43, read in full (divine sons / obeisance; angels / prevail — the pairing differs); KJV Ps 97:7, read in full via the Preview API ("worship him, all ye gods"). The Greek of Ps 97:7 (LXX 96:7) was not directly inspected.

claims.claim: The Song of Moses is poetry: it is built on parallelism (two-line verses, synonymous and synthetic), uses archaic Hebrew features, and was written colographically (in poetic layout) at Qumran — as far as is known, the first Hebrew poem so written — and on a separate scroll, testifying to its special status in that community.
claims.evidence: Nilsen, read in full (parallelism, e.g. vv. 2, 7; colography; separate scroll; archaic/archaising features); Notarius, TheTorah.com, read in part (stichographic layout at Qumran, e.g. 4QDeut-q; archaic features incl. זו zu). Probable because the Qumran layout was not directly inspected.

claims.claim: The Song's date is disputed: an archaic/early poetic core (pre-exilic, possibly pre-monarchical — Sanders, as reported by Nilsen) versus a late sixth–early fifth century scribal composition in which the archaic features are deliberate archaizing.
claims.evidence: Nilsen, read in full (reports Sanders (1996): pre-exilic, possibly pre-monarchical (before the 11th century); the 11th–4th c. range; her own conclusion: late sixth–early fifth century scribal groups; archaizing features also in younger Isaiah). The Ancient Bible World survey and the Rezetko comment are no longer relied on for this claim (see §12.3); the Albright/Robertson "late second millennium" formulation is not verified by a direct read in this session.

claims.claim: The Song's genre is disputed: farewell speech of a dying patriarch, prophetic lawsuit (rîb), or a mixed hymnic-prophetic-didactic song drawing on many genres.
claims.evidence: Nilsen, read in full (farewell-speech view pre-1950s; Wright 1962 rîb; rhetorical questions, oracles of salvation, taunts, didactic elements; resemblance to Pss 78, 105).

claims.claim: Moses and Hoshea spoke the Song, then Moses exhorted Israel to set their hearts on all the words, command them to their children, and observe all the words of the law, "for it is not a vain thing for you; because it is your life: and through this thing ye shall prolong your days in the land" (Deut 32:44–47).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:44–47, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The same day the LORD told Moses to ascend "this mountain Abarim, unto mount Nebo, which is in the land of Moab, that is over against Jericho," behold the land of Canaan, and die there and be gathered to his people, as Aaron died on Mount Hor (Deut 32:48–50).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:48–50, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The stated reason is the trespass at the waters of Meribah-Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, because Moses and Aaron sanctified God not in the midst of Israel (Deut 32:51; cf. Num 20:12–13; Num 27:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:51, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); KJV Num 20:12–13; Num 27:14, read in full via the Preview API.

claims.claim: Moses would see the land before him but not go into it (Deut 32:52).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 32:52, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: There is no direct archaeological evidence for the commission of Joshua, the writing or deposit of the law, the composition or performance of the Song, or Moses' ascent of Nebo.
claims.evidence: Dossier §6 — the negative fact, stated as such. No inscription, sanctuary, or artefact from the period can be tied to Deut 31–32.

claims.claim: The category has no independently established historical date: no year is given in Deut 31–32, and the Song's date is debated (clm-deu-09-047).
claims.evidence: Dossier §7.1; Nilsen, read in full (dating "inherently difficult").

claims.claim: Mount Nebo is traditionally identified with Jabal Nebo (modern Ras Siyagha) in Moab over against Jericho.
claims.evidence: Traditional identification; site identity and the narrated event require separate confidence judgments (Coordinator Brief, geography rule). The identification and the death narrative belong to Category 10 (Deut 33–34); no excavation has established the mountain as the place of Moses' death (see dossier §6.1).

connections.note: The commission fulfilled after Moses' death: "Be strong and of a good courage" (Josh 1:6, 7, 9); "as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee: I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee" (Josh 1:5).
The earlier designation: lay hands on Joshua, "a man in whom is the spirit," set him before Eleazar and the congregation, give him a charge in their sight.
"Charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him: for he shall go over before this people."
"For he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee" — Hebrews takes up the promise of Deut 31:6, 8.
The later public reading: Ezra brings the book of the law before the congregation, men and women, and reads from morning until midday. The ordinance's later observance, not a quotation.
The book of the law found in the house of the LORD in Josiah's reign — the narrative sequel to a deposited book; the identity of the found book with Moses' deposit is not asserted.
The foretold apostasy in its Judges setting: "the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and served Baalim… and followed other gods."
The Song commissioned (31:19–22) is the Song delivered (32:1–43).
Heaven and earth called to record — the witnesses of the covenant renewal re-invoked.

"Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the LORD hath spoken, I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me" — the same heaven-and-earth summons and the same charge of rebellion.
"The LORD is my rock" — the Rock title taken up as personal confession.
The division of the nations at Babel: "the LORD scattered them abroad… and from thence did the LORD scatter them" — the event 32:8 recalls.
The parallel allotment: the host of heaven "divided unto all nations under the whole heaven," while the LORD took Israel "out of the iron furnace… to be unto him a people of inheritance."
"Hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation" — Paul's Areopagus restatement of the Most High setting the bounds of the peoples.
"I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself" — the eagle image the Song reuses.
"Fear not, O Jacob, my servant; and thou, Jesurun, whom I have chosen" — Jeshurun again, now as the chosen and beloved, against the Song's apostate Jeshurun.
"Yea, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils" — the Psalm's retelling of the Song's charge.
"First Moses saith, I will provoke you to jealousy by them that are no people, and by a foolish nation I will anger you" — Paul quotes 32:21 and names Moses as speaker.
"For it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" — Paul quotes 32:35.
"Vengeance belongeth unto me, I will recompense, saith the Lord. And again, The Lord shall judge his people" — Hebrews quotes both 32:35 and 32:36.
"For the LORD will judge his people, and he will repent himself concerning his servants" — the same wording as 32:36, in the Psalter.

"And let all the angels of God worship him" — follows the longer Greek/Qumran form of 32:43, not the MT; exact wording is an adaptation and Ps 97:7 is a live alternative source (shared record §4; clm-deu-09-044–045).
"Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people" — Paul quotes the MT form of 32:43, the nations rejoicing with his people.
"Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua" — the name behind "Hoshea the son of Nun" in 32:44.
"Choose life… that thou mayest live" and "he is thy life, and the length of thy days" — the life/prolonged-days language the closing exhortation echoes.
"Get thee up into this mount Abarim, and see the land… thou also shalt be gathered unto thy people, as Aaron thy brother was gathered" — the same command and reason (the rebellion at Meribah).
The trespass at Meribah: "Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this congregation into the land."
"They sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb" — the Song named as the victors' song; its words are not quoted.
The Song of the Sea — the other Mosaic song, celebrating deliverance accomplished, where this Song anticipates breach and lays up a witness.
"Keep me as the apple of the eye" — the Psalm's prayer reusing the Song's image of God's keeping.
